questions.question: Explain how an earthquake happens, using the terms fault, focus, epicentre and seismic waves.
questions.expected_answer: Plate edges lock together by friction while the plates keep moving, so stress builds up in the rocks. When the stress exceeds the strength of the rock, rocks suddenly slip along a fault. The point underground where this starts is the focus; the point on the surface directly above is the epicentre. The energy released spreads out as seismic waves, causing shaking.

questions.question: Explain the difference between magnitude and intensity, and what it means that the magnitude scale is logarithmic.
questions.expected_answer: Magnitude measures the energy released by the earthquake (one value per earthquake); intensity describes the effects of shaking at a particular place (many values, decreasing with distance), on the Modified Mercalli scale. Logarithmic means each whole number up represents about ten times more ground movement and about 32 times more energy.

questions.question: Describe four effects of earthquakes and explain how a tsunami forms.
questions.expected_answer: Effects: injury and loss of life mostly from collapsing buildings; damage to infrastructure such as roads, bridges, pipes and power lines; fires from broken gas pipes and wires; disease from contaminated water and crowded shelters; displacement and homelessness; economic loss; landslides. A tsunami forms when an undersea earthquake suddenly lifts or drops the sea floor, displacing the water above; waves spread at up to about 800 km/h and grow very high in shallow coastal water.
